pages.title: Where Aberdeenshire's Ghost Stories Still Gather
pages.summary: Aberdeenshire is one of Scotland’s richest areas for haunted-place storytelling: not because every tale is equally old or equally well evidenced, but because castles, kirkyards, prisons, ballads and coastal ruins sit so close together.

pages.title: Castle Ghosts
pages.summary: Drum, Craigievar, Delgatie and Braemar show how family tragedy, romance and inheritance turn castle history into ghost lore.

pages.title: Fyvie Castle
pages.summary: Fyvie Castle brings together a Green Lady legend, a phantom trumpeter and one of the north-east's strongest haunted reputations.

pages.title: Haunted Jails
pages.summary: Peterhead Prison and Aberdeen's Tolbooth reveal how punishment sites become haunted through memory, tourism and modern investigation.

pages.title: Why Does Anglesey Feel So Haunted?
pages.summary: Anglesey’s haunted reputation is strongest where its landscape already feels charged: the unfinished walls of Beaumaris Castle, the cells of Beaumaris Gaol, the storm-beaten rock of South Stack Lighthouse, the lonely ruins around Lligwy, and the prehistoric tombs whose names still carry giant-lore.

pages.title: Castle Haunting
pages.summary: Beaumaris Castle's ghost stories draw their power from soldiers, chapel sounds and the eerie absence of an unfinished royal stronghold.

pages.title: Beaumaris Gaol
pages.summary: Beaumaris Gaol turns a disputed execution, a town clock and prison hardship into Anglesey's strongest haunted story.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index
pages.summary: Focused pages that expand on Why Does Anglesey Feel So Haunted?.

pages.title: South Stack
pages.summary: South Stack's knocking ghost legend gives Anglesey a maritime haunting shaped by storms, isolation and the fear of help arriving too late.

pages.title: Why Angus Haunts Its Old Places
pages.summary: Angus has one great public-facing haunting at its centre: Glamis Castle, the turreted ancestral seat near Forfar that is repeatedly promoted as one of Scotland’s most haunted castles.

pages.title: Glamis Castle
pages.summary: Glamis Castle is Angus's haunted showpiece, where chapel apparitions, gambling legends, hidden rooms, and family scandal gather in one place.

pages.title: Sub-Topic Index

pages.title: Montrose Ghost
pages.summary: The Montrose Ghost links a named 1913 air crash, early military aviation, and later apparition reports into Angus's most modern haunting.

pages.title: Witches & Ruins
pages.summary: Forfar Loch, Red Castle, and the Angus coast show how persecution, ruins, and dangerous landscapes become quieter local ghost traditions.

pages.title: Why Does Argyllshire Feel So Haunted?
pages.summary: Argyllshire’s haunted history is not a single tidy trail of famous “most haunted” attractions. It is a wide coastal and island tradition: castle omens at Inveraray and Dunstaffnage, the handless piper of Duntrune, massacre-memory at Glencoe, lost pipers in sea caves, fairy dogs on Tiree, and water-spirit folklore from the Hebridean edge.

pages.title: Duntrune Piper
pages.summary: Duntrune's famous piper story links clan warfare, warning music and Loch Crinan into a haunting built around sound rather than sight.

pages.title: Glencoe
pages.summary: Glencoe's haunted reputation comes from a documented massacre whose emotional weight later shaped reports of cries, shadows and fugitive figures.

pages.title: Inveraray
pages.summary: Inveraray's Grey Lady, death-omen galley and murdered harpist turn aristocratic memory into one of Argyllshire's richest ghost traditions.

pages.title: Why Does Ayrshire Feel So Haunted?
pages.summary: Ayrshire’s haunted reputation rests on an unusually strong mix of literary fame, castle folklore, witch-trial memory and coastal ruin. Its best-known supernatural landmark is Alloway Auld Kirk, made famous by Robert Burns’s Tam o’ Shanter, where witches and warlocks whirl in the ruined church before chasing Tam towards the Brig o’ Doon.

pages.title: Alloway Kirk
pages.summary: Alloway Auld Kirk became Ayrshire's defining supernatural landmark when Burns turned local witchcraft lore into Tam o' Shanter.

pages.title: Lady Ghosts
pages.summary: Ayrshire's lady apparitions link ruined castles, family memory and repeated folklore motifs from Dalquharran to Loudoun and Cassillis.

pages.title: Culzean Piper
pages.summary: Culzean's cliff caves, smuggling memories and castle apparitions make its lost piper one of Ayrshire's strongest haunted-place stories.

pages.title: Where Banffshire Keeps Its Ghost Stories
pages.summary: Banffshire’s haunted history is less a neat catalogue of “most haunted” tourist sites than a scattered north-east Scottish folklore landscape: ruined tower houses, old family seats, rivers, wells, kirkyards, mausoleums and stories preserved in local memory.

pages.title: Ballindalloch
pages.summary: Ballindalloch's Pink Lady and cellar-seeking General Grant show how family memory can become a careful castle haunting.

pages.title: Inchdrewer
pages.summary: Inchdrewer's ruined walls, Lord Banff's murder and the strange white dog make it Banffshire's darkest castle story.

pages.title: Old Folklore
pages.summary: Beyond named ghosts, Banffshire's older uncanny world includes dangerous water, healing places, fair neighbours and supernatural horses.

pages.title: Where Bedfordshire's Ghost Stories Gather
pages.summary: Bedfordshire’s haunted reputation is quieter than that of some larger counties, but it has a distinctive character: ruined churches on ridges, old monastic houses, airship sheds, coaching-road legends and country-house ghosts rather than one single headline “most haunted” attraction.

pages.title: Chicksands
pages.summary: Chicksands Priory turns monastic history into a Gothic tale of forbidden love, punishment and a ghostly nun.

pages.title: Clophill

pages.title: Road Ghosts
pages.summary: Black Tom, Odell's rider and coaching-road traditions show Bedfordshire's hauntings beyond ruined churches and old houses.

pages.title: Where Berkshire's Ghost Stories Still Linger
pages.summary: Berkshire’s haunted reputation is strongest where ordinary local history already feels charged: Windsor’s royal courts and forest, Reading’s ruined abbey, Donnington’s Civil War earthworks, Bisham’s riverside house, and Littlecote’s Tudor scandal.

pages.title: Haunted Houses

pages.summary: Reading Abbey feels haunted because execution, dissolution and scattered royal remains left a powerful historical charge.

pages.title: Windsor
pages.summary: Windsor's ghost stories mix royal death, castle tradition and the horned forest phantom made famous by Shakespeare.

pages.title: Where Berwickshire's Ghost Stories Still Linger
pages.summary: Berwickshire’s haunted history is quieter than the famous ghost circuits of Edinburgh or Northumberland, but it has a distinctive Border character: ruined coastal castles, old tower houses, vanished mansions, smuggling cellars, fishing disasters and family legends that cling to named places.

pages.title: Lost Legends
pages.summary: Houndwood, Duns Castle and other thinly sourced sites show how local legend survives when evidence is scattered.

pages.title: Where Brecknockshire's Quiet Hauntings Begin
pages.summary: Brecknockshire’s haunted reputation is quieter than that of some Welsh counties, but it has a strong atmosphere: ruined Norman castles, mountain roads, old religious sites, lonely farms, and folklore rooted in lakes, lights, goblins, and borderland memory.

pages.title: Brecon Castle
pages.summary: Brecon Castle's eerie 2016 face photograph shows how old ruins can gain new ghost stories through shadows, cameras and local news.

pages.title: Folk Lights
pages.summary: Brecknockshire's older supernatural stories centre on strange lights, goblin figures, chapel roads and journeys through uncanny uplands.

pages.title: Where Buckinghamshire's Ghost Stories Still Gather
pages.summary: Buckinghamshire’s haunted reputation is not built around one single ruin or battlefield, but around a chain of old places where social history and local storytelling cling together: the Hellfire Caves at West Wycombe, coaching inns in Aylesbury and Amersham, Tudor houses such as Chenies Manor, country estates such as Claydon and Hughenden, and older...

pages.title: Haunted Inns
pages.summary: The King's Head and the Crown show how old coaching inns turn bedrooms, servants' work and traveller gossip into enduring ghost lore.

pages.summary: Buteshire’s haunted history is best understood as an island folklore map rather than a single “most haunted county” story.

pages.title: Island Folklore
pages.summary: Beyond Brodick and Rothesay, Buteshire's eerie history lies in witchcraft, fairy belief, second sight and island fear.

pages.title: Rothesay Castle
pages.summary: Rothesay Castle's Green Lady turns Norse violence, a fatal stairway and local memory into Bute's strongest castle ghost story.

pages.title: Where Do Caernarfonshire's Ghost Stories Gather?
pages.summary: Caernarfonshire is one of Wales’s richest haunted-history landscapes: a historic county of castles, walled towns, mountain roads, slate country, old inns, coastal quays and folk traditions shaped by the borderland between memory and legend.

pages.title: Beddgelert
pages.summary: Beddgelert's haunting of David Pritchard links a restless innkeeper, hidden money and the village's famous hound legend to early Welsh tourism.

pages.title: Castle Ghosts
pages.summary: The Floating Lady story turns Caernarfon Castle's conquest history, towers and tourist memory into the county's most famous spectral landmark.

pages.title: Why Does Caithness Feel So Haunted?
pages.summary: Caithness is one of Scotland’s most atmospheric haunted-history landscapes: a far northern historic county of sea-cliffs, ruined castles, brochs, graveyards, old inns and Norse-influenced place lore.

pages.title: Broch Lore
pages.summary: Caithness's ancient brochs and mounds carry fairy lore that feels stranger and older than ordinary haunted-house tales.

pages.title: Where Does Cambridgeshire's Haunted Memory Gather?
pages.summary: Cambridgeshire’s haunted reputation is built less on ruined castles and more on places where ordinary life pressed hard against history: college courts, fenland tracks, old inns, plague-struck streets, river crossings, bookshops, parish roads and half-drained marsh.

pages.title: College Ghosts
pages.summary: Cambridge's college hauntings turn enclosed courts, old lodges and plague history into some of the county's best-known ghost traditions.

pages.title: Fen Spirits

pages.title: Road Ghosts

pages.title: Where Does Cardiganshire's Haunted Story Begin?
pages.summary: Cardiganshire, now usually called Ceredigion in modern local government, is not one of Britain’s loudest “haunted county” destinations.

pages.title: Cardigan Castle
pages.summary: Cardigan Castle mixes major Welsh history with a white lady tradition, ghost tours and the atmosphere of a restored riverside fortress.

pages.title: What Haunts Carmarthenshire's Oldest Places?
pages.summary: Carmarthenshire is one of the richest haunted-history counties in Wales because its ghost stories grow out of very old ground: medieval castles, Tudor and Georgian houses, chapel yards, courtrooms, inns, mountain lakes, and a county town long associated with Merlin.

pages.title: Where Cheshire's Ghost Stories Still Gather
pages.summary: Cheshire’s haunted reputation rests on a strong mix of old buildings, Civil War memory, country-house folklore and deliberately atmospheric tourism.

pages.title: Chester
pages.summary: Chester's ghost stories draw power from Roman walls, medieval streets, old inns and the memory of Rowton Heath.

pages.title: What Haunts Scotland's Wee County?
pages.summary: Clackmannanshire’s haunted history is not a long parade of famous ghosts. It is stranger, smaller and more local than that: a handful of powerful stories gathered around Alloa Tower, the Dollar glens, Castle Campbell, Sauchie, old wells, witch-trial memory and the dramatic edge of the Ochil Hills.

pages.title: Alloa Tower
pages.summary: Alloa Tower gathers Clackmannanshire's richest cluster of ghost stories, from chained prisoners and well legends to fire memories.

pages.title: Where Cornwall's Ghost Stories Meet History
pages.summary: Cornwall’s haunted reputation grows from three things at once: a dramatic historic county almost surrounded by sea, a deep store of recorded folklore, and a tourism landscape where ruined castles, old inns, mines, moors and tidal islands already feel half legendary.

pages.title: Bodmin Moor
pages.summary: Bodmin Moor's haunted reputation grows from murder memory, lonely pools, old tracks and folklore that clings to the landscape.

pages.title: Where Antrim's Ghost Stories Take Hold

pages.title: Where County Down Keeps Its Ghosts
pages.summary: County Down’s haunted reputation is not built around one single famous “most haunted” attraction. It is a layered landscape of castle legends, roadside apparitions, death omens, old estate stories and Troubles-era memory.

pages.title: Gill Hall

pages.summary: Cromartyshire is one of the most awkward historic counties to write about as a haunted landscape, because it was never a neat block of territory. pages.title: Where Does Haunted Denbighshire Begin?

pages.title: Why Does Derbyshire Feel So Haunted?

pages.title: Why Does Devon Feel So Haunted?

pages.title: Why Dorset Feels So Haunted
